**Setting up the problem (Bayes' theorem):**

- Prevalence: P(disease) = 1/500 = 0.002, so P(no disease) = 0.998
- Sensitivity: P(test+ | disease) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(test− | no disease) = 0.95, so P(test+ | no disease) = 0.05 (false positive rate)

**Applying Bayes' theorem:**

P(disease | test+) = [P(test+|disease)·P(disease)] / [P(test+|disease)·P(disease) + P(test+|no disease)·P(no disease)]

Numerator: 0.98 × 0.002 = 0.00196

Denominator terms:
- True positives: 0.00196
- False positives: 0.05 × 0.998 = 0.04990

Total P(test+) = 0.00196 + 0.04990 = 0.05186

P(disease | test+) = 0.00196 / 0.05186 = 0.0377941...

**Converting to percentage:** 3.7794...% ≈ **3.78%**

This illustrates the classic base-rate effect: even with a fairly sensitive and specific test, because the condition is rare, most positive results (about 96%) are false positives — the vast pool of unaffected people generates more false positives (≈49.9 per 1000 tested) than the tiny affected pool generates true positives (≈1.96 per 1000 tested).

FINAL ANSWER: 3.78
